div.head: What is a Bill of Sale?
div.p: From 1864, Bills of Sale were mortgages against personal chattels used by individuals and small businesses to raise finance. The governing Act was The Instruments and Securities Statute 1864 (27 Vict. No. 204). Schedules of the chattels were attached to the bills. The schedules list the grantors’ chattels against which a bill was drawn. When the bill was against furniture, the inventory is often given on a room-by-room basis, sometimes identify the occupant of the room. For businesses such as hotels, the chattels are of plant (including furnishings) and equipment. Bills of Sale were filed with the Registrar-General’s Department.

div.head: Where can I find Bills of Sale?
div.p: Bills of Sale are held at the Public Record Office Victoria in series VPRS 8350. This information on Bills of Sale is adapted from the PROV website.
A single sentence of 471 words in Part VII of the Act explains that Bills of Sale are to be filed in the Supreme Court. Take a breath before you read it! You can read the whole Act on AustLII.

56: Every bill of sale of personal chattels made after, the commencement of this Act either absolutely or conditionally or subject or not subject to any trusts and whereby the grantee or holder shall have power either with or without notice and either immediately after the making of such bill of sale or at any future time to seize or take possession of any property and effects comprised in or made subject to such bill of sale and every schedule or inventory which shall be thereto annexed or therein referred to or a true copy thereof respectively and of every attestation of the execution thereof shall (together with an affidavit of the time of such bill of sale being made or given and a description of the residence and occupation of the person making or giving the same or in case the same shall be made or given by any person under or in the execution of any process then a description of the residence and occupation of the person against whom such process shall have issued and of every attesting witness to such bill of sale) be filed in the office of the Registrar-General within ten days after the making or giving such bill of sale otherwise such bill of sale shall as against all assignees of the estate and effects of the person whose goods or any of them are comprised in such bill of sale under any laws now or hereafter to be in force relating to bankruptcy or insolvency or under any assignment for the benefit of the creditors of such person and as against all officers and other persons seizing any property or effects comprised in such bill of sale in the execution of any process of any court of law or equity authorizing the seizure of the goods of the person by whom or of whose goods such bill of sale shall have been made and against every person on whose behalf such process shall have been issued be null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever so far as regards the property in or right to the possession of any personal chattels comprised in such bill of sale which at or after the time of such bankruptcy or of the estate of the debtor being placed under sequestration or of the execution by the debtor of such assignment for the benefit of his creditors or of executing such process (as the case may be) and after the expiration of the said period of ten days shall be in the possession or apparent possession of the person making such bill of sale or of any person against whom the process shall have issued under or in the execution of which such bill of sale shall have been made or given as the case may be.

div.head: What sort of information will a Bill of Sale reveal?
div.p: An example of a Bill of Sale from Carlton comes from VPRS8350/P0002/95363. This is a conditional bill of sale (a chattel mortgage) dated 26 October 1892. Thomas Barker, a baker of 239 Bouverie Street, pledged the contents of his bakery and home as security for a debt to James Barker of Princes Street, Newmarket, formerly a railway employee but now retired (it’s unclear whether this is a relative, given they share the same surname).

James Barker had sold goods to Thomas, and Thomas still owed him £123 of the purchase price. The sale was made on the express condition that Thomas would give security over the goods for the unpaid balance. James appears to have sold Thomas a going bakery business, quite possibly his own on retiring, and kept a legal claim over it until he was paid.

The repayment terms were £3 a week toward the principal, starting in December 1892 — that would clear the debt in roughly 41 weeks; interest of 7% a year on the balance still owing, computed from 26 October 1892; interest paid quarterly, with the first payment due 26 January 1893.

Thomas also made the standard covenants: to keep the goods insured against fire for £120, in James’s name, with a Melbourne insurance office James approved; to pay all rents, rates and taxes on the premises; not to remove the goods from Bouverie Street without James’s written consent; and to keep the goods in good repair and let James inspect them.

Any goods Thomas later brought onto the premises for the business were also covered by the security. If Thomas defaulted, James’s powers were considerable. This included missing a payment, becoming insolvent, making an assignment to creditors, or having the goods seized by someone else. James could then enter the premises, break open doors if necessary, and seize the goods. He could sell them by auction or private sale, take his costs and the debt from the proceeds, and pay any surplus back to Thomas.
The chattels at 239 Bouverie Street that were listed in the Schedule point to a working bakery possibly with a family living on the premises.

list.item: 2 horses, each 7 years old, and 1 mare, 6 years old
2 carts, 2 complete sets of harness, 3 collars, 1 trough
6 bread trays, 2 sets of scales and weights
4 2/12 [2lb] bread tins, 7 dozen pie tins, 1 lot of bread tins
1 lot of peels [these are the long-handled wooden paddles for moving loaves in and out of the oven]
1 lot of sundries, 1 copper [a boiler], 4 tubs, 1 lot of firewood
1 double bedstead and bedding, 2 single bedsteads, 2 cots
1 wardrobe, 1 chest of drawers, 1 dresser, 1 chiffonier
1 armchair, 1 lady’s chair, 6 small chairs, 6 cane-bottomed chairs
1 washstand and ware, 2 tables, 1 round table

div.p: The horses, carts and harness suggest home bread deliveries, and the oats and chaff were feed for the horses. Barker had advertised in 1889 for a young man to drive baker’s carts. [Age, 3 Sep 1889: 8] http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article197500495

The household furniture, including two cots and two single beds, suggests Thomas lived above or behind the shop with his family. Pledging the household furniture as well as the business stock meant he had a lot to lose if the business failed. Late in 1892 Melbourne was in the grips of the land-boom collapse which may explain why a retired seller wanted his money secured so tightly, with weekly instalments and broad seizure rights.

From newspapers we can find out a little more about the business. George W. Ward sold his Bouverie Street bakery to Thomas Barker in August [1888] and moved to Elsternwick, agreeing not to carry on his trace within 5 miles of his former premises. In March 1889 Barker successfully sued Ward for breach of the agreement after Ward delivered bread to a South Melbourne address, and was award £100 and costs [Age, 21 March 1889: 5] In 1890 Barker advertised for “LAD wanted, used to horses; 15s and found” [meaning with board and lodging as well as a wage [Age, 8 Mar 1890: 5] In 1895, “BAKING Business, 13 bags. 239 Bouverie-street, Carlton” is offered for sale [Age, 17 Sep 1895: 3].
